faq.a: Start at the McBurney's point (one‑third the distance from the anterior superior iliac spine to the umbilicus); tenderness here is classic for appendicitis.
faq.q: How can I locate the appendix without imaging?

faq.a: Remove constrictive dressings, elevate the limb to heart level, and arrange urgent fasciotomy if signs progress.
faq.q: What is the first step in managing a suspected compartment syndrome?

faq.a: The femoral artery lies outside the fascial compartment; loss of distal pulses occurs only when swelling extends beyond the fascia.
faq.q: Why is the femoral pulse still palpable in a thigh compartment syndrome?

exam: A 25‑year‑old farmer presents with right upper quadrant pain after a fall; what anatomical landmark helps you differentiate hepatic injury from gallbladder disease? — Identify the liver’s right mid‑clavicular line border; tenderness below this suggests hepatic contusion, while a positive Murphy’s sign points to gallbladder pathology.

During a trauma assessment you find a firm, tender swelling on the anterior thigh; what compartment is most likely involved and why? — The anterior compartment (quadriceps) is enclosed by the fascia lata; swelling there produces pain on passive knee flexion and threatens the femoral nerve.

A patient with severe malaria develops respiratory distress; which diaphragmatic landmark guides your bedside assessment of pleural effusion? — Use the costal margin at the mid‑axillary line; dullness below this on percussion indicates fluid accumulation.

You need to locate the femoral nerve for a nerve block but lack ultrasound; which surface anatomy clues do you use? — Palpate the femoral pulse in the femoral triangle, then move laterally 1‑2 cm; the nerve lies just lateral to the artery under the fascia.

A child presents with a swollen, painful calf after a long walk; how does anatomy help you rule out deep vein thrombosis in a low‑resource setting? — Examine for Homan’s sign (pain on dorsiflexion) and assess for calf tenderness over the posterior tibial vessels; absence of these makes DVT less likely.

In a patient with suspected perforated duodenal ulcer, which anatomical relationship explains the risk of retroperitoneal infection? — The second part of the duodenum lies posterior to the portal vein and inferior vena cava; perforation can spread infection to the retroperitoneal space.
ai.title: Human Anatomy for Diploma Students
ai.subject: Anatomy
ai.summary: A concise overview of gross anatomy relevant to diploma‑level clinicians in low‑resource settings. Emphasises clinical landmarks, common injuries and exam strategies for ward rounds.

b: Focus on palpable structures and easily visualised regions.
Prioritise knowledge that changes immediate patient management.
sections.p: Anatomy provides the map for every clinical encounter. Knowing surface landmarks, organ positions and relationships guides history, examination, procedures and interpretation of limited investigations.

b: Thoracic inlet: clavicle, sternum, first rib.
Abdominal quadrants: right upper – liver, gallbladder; left lower – sigmoid colon.
sections.p: Key regions include the thorax, abdomen, pelvis and extremities. Recognise the vertebral levels of the diaphragm (T8‑T10) and the aortic bifurcation (L4).

b: Femoral triangle: femoral nerve, artery, vein, then lymphatics (N‑A‑V‑L).
Carotid sheath: common carotid artery, internal jugular vein, vagus nerve.
sections.p: Understanding what lies adjacent to a structure predicts spread of infection or injury. For example, the duodenum’s second part lies anterior to the inferior vena cava and posterior to the portal vein.

b: Abdomen: abdominal aorta gives celiac trunk, SMA, IMA.
sections.p: Identify the main arterial sources for each region; this guides resuscitation and surgical planning when imaging is unavailable.

b: Sciatic nerve compression → posterior thigh pain, foot drop.
sections.p: Peripheral nerves convey sensory clues and motor deficits. The femoral nerve supplies the anterior thigh and knee extension; loss suggests a high lumbar plexus lesion.

b: Peritoneal reflections create potential spaces for fluid accumulation.
Ligamentous support of the pelvis limits organ prolapse.
sections.p: Anatomical structures have predictable functions that explain clinical signs. The diaphragm’s contraction creates negative intrathoracic pressure, essential for ventilation.

b: Blunt abdominal trauma → look for seat‑belt sign, guarding, hypotension.
Compartment syndrome: pain out of proportion, tense swelling, loss of distal pulses.
sections.p: Common low‑resource presentations include abdominal trauma, peripheral nerve palsies from machete injuries, and compartment syndrome after prolonged immobilisation.

t.a: Focused Assessment with Sonography for Trauma (FAST)
t.b: Detects intra‑abdominal free fluid when CT is unavailable; a positive scan indicates hemoperitoneum requiring urgent surgery.
Assesses oxygenation in respiratory compromise; if unavailable, observe cyanosis and respiratory rate.

b: Palpate the liver edge at the right mid‑clavicular line; >2 cm below the costal margin suggests hepatomegaly.
Assess for shifting dullness to identify ascites when ultrasound is not possible.
sections.p: During ward rounds, link anatomy to the patient’s story. Use a systematic head‑to‑toe approach, confirming landmarks before ordering tests.

whenToSeekHelp: Sudden loss of consciousness with unequal pupils
Severe abdominal distension with absent bowel sounds and hypotension
Rapidly expanding limb swelling with pain and paresthesia
